title: Methodology
paragraphs: Chapter 5 Methodology Chapter abstract. This chapter details the eld wave, the calibration procedure, and the in-silico procedure. It explains sampling, consent, ride context, the listening episode, questionnaire blocks, the 60-to-52 screen, and quality checks. It then explains the embedding, debiasing, manifold, persona, factorial ABM, and measurement steps, with plain-language notes on each formal stage. It states the design limitations and the analysis-plan discipline. The empirical programme combines quantitative and qualitative eld material, then distinguishes these human records from model-based evidence. The rst is a measured eld wave, a cross-sectional questionnaire administered to university students who listen to social media radio during rides with Uber, accompanied by 60 researcher-recorded qualitative case accounts. The questionnaire provides audience and measurement summaries and supplies the target distribution for calibration. The second is a calibrated in-silico experiment, a two-arm agent-based simulation representing alternative platform congurations whose parameters were calibrated to the measured wave, which supplies a model-conditional architectural counterfactual. A further LLM-agent platform extension is specied but has not been conducted. A separate synthesis of prototype FGD narratives informs prospective rule-based 81

CHAPTER 5. METHODOLOGY 82 and LLM-agent design without adding participants to the eld wave. This chapter describes the evidence sources and their integration. Their separation is maintained throughout: measured values are reported as measured, and simulated values are reported as counterfactual estimates. 5.1 Ethical Protocol The supplied F1.0 questionnaire states voluntary participation, academic use, the option to skip items, and anonymous aggregate reporting. These are the instrument's stated conditions, not proof of completed institutional approval. The separate prole archive includes names and contextual descriptions; therefore the linked research archive must be treated as identiable or pseudonymised rather than wholly anonymous. This thesis reports only case codes and limited excerpts, not names, detailed biographies, or trip traces. The researcher must reconcile consent for linking notes to questionnaires and for quoting recorded remarks with the original information given to students. Permission for an academic questionnaire does not automatically authorise uploading proles to an external LLM service. The planned agent extension requires a separately approved data-use and de-identication procedure. Institutional authorisation is distinct from the consent wording and is not established by the statistical les. No approval decision is inferred from the presence of data.

CHAPTER 5. METHODOLOGY 83 5.2 The Measured Study 5.2.1 Participants and Sampling The target population was university students who listen to social media radio, in Egypt, while riding with Uber in the October 6th City area, Giza. This venue was chosen because it concentrates precisely the epistemic conditions the framework addresses: a bounded attention window, a social context, and exposure to broadcast content through the drivers' or riders' devices. The planning calculation is documented in Appendix E; it is not evidence of power for an independent-groups eld experiment. A convenience sample of 60 respondents was recruited. The supplied form asks respondents to consider a broadcast heard during a ride and explicitly excludes ACU students. A seven-day eligibility window is not documented in that form and is not imposed retrospectively. The historical analysis excluded eight records, leaving N = 52 (30 male, 22 female). The analysis export contains six institutional categories, with category counts of 3 to 13; no single category constitutes a majority of the sample. All 52 records contribute to the pooled analyses. Identical answers alone cannot establish that two records belong to the same person, so the exclusion rule is a limitation as well as a data-processing step. The newly supplied processing specication identies a 21-eld response-and-context key that reproduces the retained sample (Section 6.4). The participant ow is shown in Figure 5.1.

It does not provide an expert-panel voting matrix, cognitive-interview record, or independent translation-validation study. Boateng et al. (2018) distinguish item development, scale construction, and scale evaluation; evidence from one stage cannot replace another. Here internal consistency and factor t assess properties of the recorded responses, not completed content validation. The English and Arabic wording is reproduced without claiming that the two versions have demonstrated measurement equivalence. PB3's comparative trust and PB4's structural clarity must not be relabelled as verication intention and inuence of a displayed score. The latter interpretations in earlier drafts did not match the supplied instrument. 5.2.4 Procedure Respondents completed the questionnaire on a mobile device at the end of a social media radio listening episode during a ride. Completion followed the consent screen. The star rating and the PB battery were completed as separate blocks. This separation does not eliminate common-source covariance, response styles, or a general favourable impression (Podsako et al., 2024). The supplied les do not establish exact administration timestamps or independently certify that every note was recorded contemporaneously.

CHAPTER 5. METHODOLOGY 86 5.2.5 The Ecological Momentary Assessment Schedule The platform design species four measurement windows: pre-broadcast (PR1 PR3), post-broadcast (PB1PB5 and star rating), echo-triggered (EM1EM3), and weekly (WK1WK15). The proposed post-broadcast trigger is within 30 seconds of an episode ending, and the echo trigger is linked to the platform's diversity indicator. These timing rules describe the intended EMA implementation, rather than a longitudinal design completed by the 52-person survey. The supplied cross-sectional exports do not contain session timestamps with which to assess compliance with a 30-second window. Accordingly, the present results are described as post-broadcast questionnaire results, not as demonstrated longitudinal or real-time behavioural effects. 5.2.6 Analysis Psychometric analysis used internal-consistency coecients (Cronbach's α and a standardized one-factor model-based omega, exported as omega_bpa), corrected item-total correlations with the specied retention oor of r ≥0.30, Spearman associations with the separate, same-respondent star rating and with behaviourally relevant covariates (ride duration, interaction level), and conrmatory factor analysis where the sample permitted. The small-sample strategy accepted exploratory use of CFA with explicit reporting of t: the ve-item single-factor PB battery and the eleven-item BRS were evaluated with t reported honestly, without assuming a saturated solution before the N = 52 data were tted, and the single-factor result is reported regardless of t. No completed invariance test is present in the supplied

CHAPTER 5. METHODOLOGY 87 exports. Group gures therefore describe observed scores, not comparable latent means. Any later human latent-mean comparison would require a defensible measurement structure and appropriate loading and intercept or threshold comparisons (Putnick & Bornstein, 2016). 5.3 Mixed-Methods Design and Qualitative Corpus The completed empirical report combines a quantitative questionnaire analysis with a qualitative analysis of researcher-recorded ride encounters. Integration was undertaken during this thesis revision, after the quantitative summaries were available; it is not retrospectively described as a prospectively registered convergent design. The purpose of mixing is complementarity and examination of tensions: what makes an experience worthwhile, and when do numerical ratings or activity categories omit that meaning? Creswell and Plano Clark (2018) and Levitt et al. (2018) motivate specifying the purpose, timing, and point of integration rather than simply placing two datasets side by side. RQ5 (Qualitative experience). How do the rider records describe credibility, listening value, participation, and platform experience? RQ6 (Integration). Where do these accounts converge with, complement, or challenge the paired questionnaire ratings? These additional exploratory questions organise the newly integrated analysis and are separate from the original H1H7 hypotheses. The source corpus contains 60 case records in the rider-account corpus, with observations, recorded remarks, and researcher reections, alongside duration, mood, and interaction descriptors. All 60 have distinct identiers and nonempty

CHAPTER 5. METHODOLOGY 88 text. The 52 identiers in the retained quantitative response matrix dene the paired quantitativequalitative subset. The eight other notes remain in the qualitative corpus: exclusion from a historical numeric analysis does not establish that a distinct narrative is invalid. Results report both denominators without treating them as independent samples. the contextual student proles provides biographical and media-preference descriptions of the same case series; it is not another sample. Some identiers use dierent zero-padding from the CSV les. Proles are contextual documents and candidate future anchors, not an independent source of corroboration or an extra set of interview responses. The 25 topics in the programme-topic proposals are proposed content stimuli, not 25 additional observations or completed recordings. 5.3.1 Analytical Position and Coding Procedure The analysis of the 60 rider records is a semantic, codebook-based thematic analysis, with the assistance disclosed in the opening declaration, of recorded accounts. It is informed by the distinctions among approaches to analysis discussed by Braun and Clarke (2019), and by Kiger and Varpio's (2020) account of developing and reviewing themes. It is not described as independent human coding or a reliability-tested content analysis of those records. A separate 193-segment FGD/self-report codebook validation used three independent coders and is reported in Section 6.12.15. The primary coding units were the key_observations and notable_quotes elds. The researcher_reflections eld was read as interpretation, not counted as independent participant testimony. Familiarisation distinguished observable actions, attributed remarks, and inferences about personality or platform success.

CHAPTER 5. METHODOLOGY 89 Initial semantic codes concerned correction, source use, social endorsement, familiar voices, calm, time t, agency, local relevance, and technical usability. These were grouped into six themes, checked against the complete case inventory, and recorded with an inclusion rule, exclusion rule, and case-level memo. A case could receive multiple codes. Coding decisions are explicit in the case-level coding record; the thematic codebook denes the themes, and Appendix F provides the membership matrix. The counts describe the reach of this coding within the supplied records; they are not population prevalence estimates or measures of thematic importance. The script joins codes to source identiers, calculates counts for 60 and 52 records, and veries selected numerical summaries. It does not discover themes by keyword frequency. For the 60 rider records, no second-coder agreement, member checking, thematic saturation, or participant validation is claimed. The separate validation provides coder agreement for the 25-code FGD/self-report codebook, not for the rider-record themes. The audit retains source excerpts and interpretive decisions so the analysis can be examined. 5.3.2 Integration and Qualitative Trustworthiness A joint display combines selected case accounts with the same cases' PB scores and interaction categories. It considers convergence, elaboration, and tension, not whether each quotation conrms EST. Quiet appreciation, conditional preference, and a request for better topic lters were retained rather than excluded as inconvenient cases. The small purposive illustrations do not support subgroup signicance tests.

CHAPTER 5. METHODOLOGY 90 The records are polished, predominantly favourable English narratives with recurrent links between academic discipline and media preference. That style limits how closely they can be treated as spontaneous speech. The archive does not establish whether every attributed quotation is verbatim, translated, or reconstructed. Excerpts are therefore identied as recorded remarks, not certied interview transcripts. Positive descriptions cannot establish absence of dissatisfaction, and a researcher's explanation of a student's motives is not direct access to that student's experience. This is a complete analysis of the supplied case corpus, not a claim of exhaustive understanding of the wider student population. The questionnaire's promise of anonymity must be distinguished from the identiable prole archive. Names and detailed backstories are not reproduced in the results. Publication, retention, and later LLM processing require a consent and access review. No prole data were sent to external model APIs for the proposed experiment during this revision. 5.4 Focus-Group Evidence and Its Role in the Study The prototype FGD is separate from the rider records in Section 5.3. Two overlapping narratives describe one reported university wireframe walkthrough; they are not two samples and are not added to the 60 rider accounts or 52 retained questionnaires. Participant overlap is unknown. Appendix G contains the full merged report, codebook, recording audit, and interpretive limits. The accounts describe Egyptian Arabic discussion, an ACU context, smartphone wireframes, and an approximately 28-minute session. The more precise re-

CHAPTER 5. METHODOLOGY 91 ported duration is 1,675.33 seconds, not metadata independently measured here. The transcript, recording, roster, and consent documentation remain absent. The analysis is consequently a critical synthesis of reported narratives, not newly completed transcript-level coding. Its four domains, FGD-T1FGD-T4, remain distinct from the rider corpus's T1T6 codes. A supplemental le, fgd_analysis_parts.json, supplies seven generated text summaries, not an original transcript, frame log, or additional sample. Its candidate extracts contain translation inconsistencies, malformed intervals, and uncertain speaker labels. The review accepts the existence of the export and retains programme-length and registration-feedback questions for later source checking; it does not accept claims that the primary records have been recovered. The decision record is summarised in Appendix G.4. Model-use provenance is disclosed in the opening declaration. No new inductive transcript coding or audiovisual triangulation is claimed. Focus groups require attention to interaction, not an assumption that a moderator's explanation constitutes participant endorsement (Kitzinger, 1995). The synthesis separates reported experience, interpretation, competing explanations, and implications. No quotations, theme prevalence, saturation, or coding reliability are invented. COREQ and APA qualitative reporting guidance inform the documentation checks without certifying missing procedures (Levitt et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2007).

CHAPTER 5. METHODOLOGY 92 5.4.1 Empirical Anchors, Assumptions, and Factual Ground Truth Empirical anchors are source-linked human accounts or observations used within their evidentiary limits. Design assumptions are proposed mechanisms or scenario settings. Factual ground truth refers more narrowly to independently adjudicated answers for a dened assessment task. A preference for co-hosting is not a veried answer to a news claim, and a theme is not an estimated transition probability. The FGD currently supplies provisional design hypotheses, not veried individual personas, numerical calibration targets, or factual answer keys. Its repeated lexical counts are retained for audit only. New extracts must enter the evidence register with locators, speaker roles, quotation/translation status, permission scope, and coding decisions before participant-level use. Assessment keys and held-out outcomes remain outside participant-agent prompts. CHAPTER 5. METHODOLOGY 93 5.5 The Calibrated In-Silico Experiment (Final Pipeline) The nal computational study is a calibrated in-silico experiment, not a eld intervention. It has three stages: (1) four-stream embedding, machine-learning debiasing, and Monte-Carlo prior construction; (2) a within-persona 23 full-factorial tensor agent-based model (ABM) with eight mathematical inuence lters and a Zewail-inspired attentional gate; and (3) a GRM-IRT measurement model with dual frequentist and Bayesian inference, adversarial stress tests, and global sensitivity analysis. The complete implementation, data, seeds, and generated outputs are included in the reproducibility archive (Appendix K). The pipeline is deliberately explicit about what it can and cannot identify. The measured wave anchors the prior and the measurement model. The architectural contrast is a counterfactual generated within the model. No simulation output is relabelled as a human treatment eect. What is assumed and what is estimated. The empirical streams anchor the persona distribution, the measurement model, and the semantic features. The treatment coecients in the outcome equations (for example 0.42 for A, 0.28 for B, and 0.32 for C on credibility; 0.35, 0.26, and 0.40 on competence; and −0.05, −0.11, and −0.06 on engagement) are design assumptions. They are not estimated from the 52 respondents. The simulation propagates those assumptions through the ABM and the measurement model; it does not identify a eld treatment eect. The value of the exercise lies in the internal consistency of the implied design, the epistemic engagement trade-o, and the sensitivity of the implied results to the declared mech-

CHAPTER 5. METHODOLOGY 96 Sentence-transformer architecture and process. The encoder is BAAI/ bge-m3, a multilingual sentence-transformer built on an XLM-RoBERTa backbone. It returns a 1,024-dimensional dense sentence vector and supports long inputs up to 8,192 tokens. The thesis uses the dense embedding only; the model's sparse and multi-vector outputs are not used. The encoder is used zero-shot: it is not ne-tuned on the thesis data, and no supervised label enters the embedding step. The process is: (1) assemble the 5,258 document texts and their source metadata; (2) clean and truncate each text to the model limit; (3) tokenise and encode mini-batches on the Colab T4 in mixed precision; (4) pool and L2-normalise the dense representation; (5) cache the vectors by a hash of the model name and document set; and (6) project the semantic block to 32 principal components, which enter the 198-feature matrix alongside the 31 quantitative features. The cache makes the run reproducible without a second API call. This is a measurement pipeline, not a claim that the 1,024 dimensions are psychological constructs; the cosine diagnostics in Section 5.5.4 show moderate, not clean, stream separation. It does not establish that the six axes are uniquely identied psychological constructs. 5.5.3 Stage 1: Monte-Carlo Prior Q0 and Random Personas A continuous prior Q0(θ) is tted to the debiased coordinates. When the sample covariance is well conditioned, a Gaussian kernel density estimator is used; otherwise a shrunken multivariate normal is substituted. The generator draws n = 500 personas, θa ∼Q0, and maps the six latent axes to the ABM traits (initial opinion, prior reputation, echo susceptibility, heat capacity, critical scrutiny, and co-hosting preference). Every persona is cloned across all eight factorial cells, so within-persona contrasts are paired by construction. The n = 500 personas are a computational population, not 500 additional human respondents. Who the synthetic personas represent. The personas are drawn after DML/IPW and after the six-axis spectral projection, so they inherit the debiased latent geometry of the 52 measured students, not the raw questionnaire rows. The measured anchor is a convenience sample of university students who were Uber riders in the October 6th City area, Giza: age mean 20.37 (SD 0.95; range 1923), 30 male and 22 female respondents, academic years 14, and eight faculties across six universities.
